newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Accused Colombian drug baron nabbed in Venezuela.
newsitem.headline: Accused Colombian drug baron nabbed in Venezuela.

text.p: A reputed Colombian drug baron described as the top drug lord still on the run was arrested on Friday in Venezuela, a capture Colombian President Ernesto Samper called the end of the major leagues of drug trafficking.
Justo Pastor Perafan, described as the wealthiest and most wanted man in Colombia, was arrested in San Cristobal, capital of Tachira state, just across the border from Colombia.
His personal fortune has been estimated at $12 billion by Colombia's respected news magazine Semana, with vast business interests extending to Madrid, Rome, Moscow and South Africa.
Perafan, 50, had been actively sought for more than a year in Colombia, where police posted a $500,000 reward for information leading to his arrest.
"With his capture we have ended what we could call the big leagues of drug trafficking in Colombia," Samper told reporters in the central city of Pereira.
After the arrest of the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers and most other Cali drug cartel leaders in 1995 and 1996, Perafan was allegedly the top Colombian drug lord still at large.

Perafan, who had apparently been living in San Cristobal for about a year under a false identity, was flown to Caracas. He arrived at the Francisco de Miranda air base in central Caracas amid tight security, witnesses said, and was being held at military intelligence headquarters.

Samper said that if Venezuela chose not to deport Perafan, Colombia would officially seek his extradition. But Colombian Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia did not rule out that Venezuela may extradite him to the United States instead.

"He has a criminal record in that country too," she said, confirming that Perafan is wanted on drug charges in New York. He is also sought in Costa Rica and Panama where he was picked up in 1982 but slipped away without facing charges.
U.S. Ambassador to Colombia Myles Frechette said Washington was undecided whether to put forward an extradition request.

Gen. Gerardo Briceno, a commander of Venezuela's National Guard in San Cristobal, said Perafan did not resist arrest when police detained him at around 1 a.m. (0500 GMT) at a small commercial center, capping months of intelligence work.
Colombian police sources said a San Cristobal resident tipped authorities to Perafan's whereabouts after seeing his picture in a copy of Colombia's Cromos news magazine.
From his cell in San Cristobal, Perafan emphatically denied he had anything to do with drugs and said he was "unjustly persecuted in Colombia for political reasons."
"I am not a drug trafficker, never been one and never will be one. I'm just an honest businessman," he said.
Colombian National Police chief Rosso Jose Serrano, who flew to San Cristobal before dawn and helped identify Perafan, noted that all drug traffickers claimed their innocence.
"We're very happy, just as happy as if we had captured him ourselves, because we have him behind bars," he said.
Perafan has been accused of shipping more than 4,400 pounds (2,000 kg) of cocaine to Italy and other countries.
